meta.title: URL Shortener
meta.summary: Turn long URLs into short codes and redirect at very high read volume.

functional: Create a short link for a long URL
Redirect a short link to its long URL

slos.name: Redirect availability
slos.sli: Redirects answered with a 2xx or 3xx, divided by all redirect requests, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Redirect speed
slos.sli: Redirects served within the threshold, divided by all redirects, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Link creation
slos.sli: Successful creates divided by create attempts, measured at the API

alerts.when: Redirect errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Users are getting broken links right now. Alerting on the burn rate pages quickly for a real outage and ignores brief blips.

alerts.when: p99 redirect latency above 100 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Redirects are the whole product; slow ones feel broken.

alerts.when: Cache hit ratio below 90% for 30 minutes
alerts.why: Not visible to users yet, but every miss becomes a database read. Fix it before latency suffers.

alerts.when: Replica lag above 5 seconds for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Lagging replicas return stale or missing links right after a link is created.
If keys run out, every create fails. Refill automatically, and ticket it if the pool keeps falling.

signals.name: Unissued keys remaining
signals.why: The one resource that, if exhausted, breaks every write.

signals.name: Hit ratio
signals.why: Redirects are 100:1 reads, so the hit ratio decides how much reaches the database.

signals.name: Replication lag
signals.why: Replicas are written asynchronously: lag is the price of cheap reads.

steps: Open the SLO dashboard: is it every region or just one?
Check the cache hit ratio. A drop means the database is answering more of the reads.
Open a slow trace and find the longest span: cache, replica or network?
If the replica span is long, check replica lag and connection counts.
Look for a viral link: one hot key can overload a single cache shard.
Check the key pool: an empty pool means the key generator cannot issue codes.
Look at primary database errors and connection saturation.
Check recent deploys of the API and the key generator.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the short domain at the CDN

flows.title: Create link
flows.summary: Write path: the client submits a long URL and gets back a short code.

steps.label: resolve sho.rt
steps.detail: DNS points the short domain at the CDN, which answers from the nearest edge location. Browsers and resolvers cache the answer, so most clicks skip this lookup entirely.

steps.label: POST /api/links
steps.detail: The browser sends the long URL. Every request enters through the nearest CDN edge, which terminates TLS.
steps.payload:
POST /api/links HTTP/2
Host: sho.rt
Content-Type: application/json

{ "url": "https://example.com/some/very/long/path?utm_source=…" }

steps.label: POST: never cached
steps.detail: Writes bypass the cache entirely. The CDN still adds value: TLS close to the user and DDoS absorption.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: The load balancer is the single public origin. It health-checks API instances and routes only to healthy ones.

steps.label: route → api-1
steps.detail: Any instance can take the request. Stateless servers are what let us scale out horizontally.

steps.label: next key
steps.detail: Rather than hash the URL and check for collisions, take a pre-generated unique key. KGS hands each API instance a batch of keys, so this is usually an in-memory pop.

steps.label: "aZ3k9Q"
steps.detail: 6 base62 chars → 62⁶ ≈ 56.8B codes. A key batch is marked used atomically when issued, so two servers never get the same key.

steps.label: INSERT link
steps.detail: The primary is the source of truth. The short code is the primary key, so every later lookup is a single index seek.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO links (code, long_url, created_at)
VALUES ('aZ3k9Q', 'https://example.com/…', now());

steps.label: COMMIT ok
steps.detail: Durable once committed to the primary.

steps.label: replicate (WAL)
steps.detail: Replication is asynchronous: the write was acknowledged before replicas have it. A read hitting a replica in the next few ms could miss, which is why we warm the cache next.

steps.label: SET aZ3k9Q ttl=24h
steps.detail: Write-through warm-up: freshly created links are clicked almost immediately (the creator tests it), and this hides replica lag.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: Return the short URL.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: Back out through the load balancer.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: Done. Server-side cost is dominated by the DB commit (~5–10 ms); the user sees roughly one network round trip on top.

flows.title: Redirect (cache hit)
flows.summary: The hot path, ~99% of traffic: resolve a code from cache and redirect.

steps.label: resolve sho.rt
steps.detail: DNS points the short domain at the CDN, which answers from the nearest edge location. Browsers and resolvers cache the answer, so most clicks skip this lookup entirely.

steps.label: GET /aZ3k9Q
steps.detail: Someone clicks the short link. DNS points sho.rt at the nearest CDN edge, which terminates TLS.
steps.payload:
GET /aZ3k9Q HTTP/2
Host: sho.rt
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 …
Referer: https://twitter.com/

steps.label: MISS: 302s not cached
steps.detail: Trade-off: a 301 cached at the CDN and in browsers is fastest, but then the origin never sees the click. We return 302 + no-store so every click is counted. Use 301 if analytics don't matter.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: The CDN forwards over a pooled, already-warm connection to the origin, saving a TLS handshake per request.

steps.label: route → api-2
steps.detail: Least-outstanding-requests routing. API servers are stateless, so any healthy instance can serve any request.

steps.label: GET aZ3k9Q
steps.detail: Check the cache first (cache-aside).

steps.label: HIT → long URL
steps.detail: Link popularity is heavily skewed, so a cache holding the hot set answers most redirects in under a millisecond without touching the database.

steps.label: publish click
steps.detail: Fire-and-forget: the API publishes and does not wait. A slow analytics pipeline can never slow down a redirect.

steps.label: 302 Found
steps.detail: The API answers with a redirect. Total time inside the origin is a couple of milliseconds.

steps.label: 302 Found
steps.detail: Response travels back through the load balancer.

steps.label: 302 → long URL
steps.detail: Browser follows Location. The user is gone; everything after this is background work.

steps.label: deliver batch (500)
steps.detail: Workers pull events in batches. If they fall behind, the queue absorbs the backlog instead of the API.

steps.label: INSERT batch
steps.detail: Aggregated into a columnar store for dashboards: clicks per link per hour, referrers, countries.

flows.title: Redirect (cache miss)
flows.summary: A cold link: fall back to a read replica, then populate the cache.

steps.label: GET /aZ3k9Q
steps.detail: Someone clicks the short link. DNS points sho.rt at the nearest CDN edge, which terminates TLS.
steps.payload:
GET /aZ3k9Q HTTP/2
Host: sho.rt
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 …
Referer: https://twitter.com/

steps.label: MISS: 302s not cached
steps.detail: Trade-off: a 301 cached at the CDN and in browsers is fastest, but then the origin never sees the click. We return 302 + no-store so every click is counted. Use 301 if analytics don't matter.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: The CDN forwards over a pooled, already-warm connection to the origin, saving a TLS handshake per request.

steps.label: route → api-2
steps.detail: Least-outstanding-requests routing. API servers are stateless, so any healthy instance can serve any request.

steps.label: GET aZ3k9Q
steps.detail: Check the cache first.

steps.label: MISS
steps.detail: Cold or evicted link.

steps.label: SELECT long_url
steps.detail: Reads go to replicas so the primary only handles writes. At 100:1 read:write this is where read capacity scales.
steps.payload: SELECT long_url FROM links WHERE code = 'aZ3k9Q';

steps.label: row
steps.detail: Single primary-key lookup, ~1–2 ms.

steps.label: SET ttl=24h
steps.detail: Populate on miss so the next click is a hit. The TTL bounds staleness if a link is edited or deleted.

steps.label: 302 Found
steps.detail: The API answers with a redirect. Total time inside the origin is a couple of milliseconds.

steps.label: 302 Found
steps.detail: Response travels back through the load balancer.

steps.label: 302 → long URL
steps.detail: Slightly slower than a hit (extra DB round trip), still well within the 100 ms budget.

notes.text: Pre-generated keys avoid hash collisions and retry loops. Alternative: base62(counter) per range-allocated instance; simpler but codes become guessable.
302 + no-store keeps every click visible to analytics. 301 would let browsers and the CDN serve repeats, cutting origin load at the cost of click counts.
Reads dominate 100:1. Replicas scale reads; cache absorbs the hot set. Replica lag is hidden by warming the cache on create.
~3 TB over 5 years fits one primary; shard by code hash only if write volume grows by orders of magnitude.
If analytics is down, events back up in the queue; redirects are unaffected.

Only the load balancer is in public subnets. API servers, caches and databases have no public IPs; the API reaches the queue through a private endpoint, and security groups only allow LB → API → data on the needed ports.
Every tier spans 3 availability zones: losing one zone removes a third of capacity, the database fails over to a replica in another zone, and redirects keep working.

questions.q: How do you guarantee short codes never collide when many API servers create links at once?
questions.a: Hand out codes that are unique by construction instead of checking after the fact. The key generation service pre-allocates ranges (or batches of random codes) to each API server, so two servers never issue the same code and no write has to retry. A unique index on the code in the database is the safety net, not the mechanism.

questions.q: A link goes viral and its cache entry expires. What happens, and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Thousands of concurrent misses all hit the database for the same key at once, a cache stampede. Coalesce the misses so only one request refills the entry (a lock or single-flight per key), serve the stale value while it refreshes, and add jitter to expiry times. Reads that do reach storage go to the read replica, not the primary.

questions.q: Should the redirect be a 301 or a 302?
questions.a: A 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load and latency but means repeat clicks never reach you, so click counts undercount. A 302 sends every click through the service, so analytics are complete at the cost of more traffic. Most shorteners that sell analytics use 302 and lean on the CDN and cache for speed.

questions.q: Why is click counting asynchronous, and what happens if the analytics pipeline is down?
questions.a: Counting a click must never slow down or break a redirect, so the API only drops an event on the queue and responds. If the workers or the analytics store are down, events wait in the queue and are processed when they recover; counts are late, not lost, as long as the queue retention covers the outage.

questions.q: A user creates a link and clicks it immediately, but the redirect returns 404. Why?
questions.a: The read went to a replica that had not caught up with the primary yet. Fix it by writing the new mapping to the cache as part of the create call, or by reading from the primary for a short window after a write. Read-your-own-writes matters here; eventual consistency for other users is fine.

questions.q: How would you support links that expire, and clean up old ones?
questions.a: Store an expiry time with each link and check it on redirect, so an expired link stops working immediately even before cleanup. Remove expired rows lazily on read and with a background job in small batches, so cleanup never competes with live traffic. Freed codes should not be reused for a while to avoid sending old links somewhere new.
